103522	Problem 6-4. [10 points] Conservative Cycles
103523	In Wentonian physics, a force field acts on the motion of a particle by requiring a certain positive
103524	or negative amount of work to move along any path. A force field is conservative if the total sum
103525	of work is zero along every closed loop. Given a discrete force field represented by n possible
103526	particle locations `i and O(n) possible particle transitions1, where transition (`i, `j , wij ) moves a
103527	particle along a directed path from location `i to location `j requiring (positive or negative) integer
103528	work wij , describe an O(n2)-time algorithm to determine whether the force field is conservative.
103529	1Note that a transition from `i to `j does not imply the existence of a transition from `j to `i.
103530	4 Problem Set 6
103531	Solution: Construct a graph G with a vertex for each particle location `i and a directed edge (`i, `j )
103532	of weight wij for each transition (`i, `j , wij ). We can refute that the force field is conservative by
103533	finding a cycle in G that has non-zero weight. Add a supernode s connected to every v ∈ V with
103534	a directed zero-weight edge (s, v) (which does not add any new cycles to the graph). Then, run
103535	Bellman-Ford from s to determine whether there are any negative-weight cycles; then negate all
103536	edges weights and run Bellman-Ford from s again to determine whether there are any negative￾weight cycles (positive-weight cycles in the original graph). If Bellman-Ford detects either type of
103537	cycle, we can return that the force is not conservative (since we have found a cycle with non-zero
103538	weight); otherwise no non-zero weight cycles exist, so we can return that the field is conservative.
103539	Since we only add one node and O(|n|) edges to a graph with n vertices and O(n) edges, Bellman￾Ford will take O(n2) time, as desired.
103540	Note that it is possible to solve this problem in O(n) time using algorithms we have not learned in
103541	this class, but this is beyond the scope of this class. Namely:
103542	• identify the strongly connected components (SCCs) of G in O(n) time via a modified DFS;
103543	• use DFS within each SSC to assign shortest-path length potentials to each vertex;
103544	• and then check each edge of each SCC against these potentials in O(n) time.
103545	Rubric:
103546	• 3 points for description of a correct algorithm
103547	• 2 points for a correct argument of correctness
103548	• 2 points for a correct argument of running time
103549	• 3 points if correct algorithm is efficient, i.e., O(n2)
103550	• Partial credit may be awarded
103551	Problem 6-5. [20 points] SparkPlug Derby
103552	LightQueen McNing is a race car that wants to drive to California to compete in a road race: the
103553	annual SparkPlug Derby. She has a map depicting:
103554	• the n intersections in the country, where each intersection xi is marked with its positive
103555	integer elevation ei and whether it contains a gas station; and
103556	• the r roads connecting pairs of them, where each road rj is marked with the positive integer
103557	tj denoting the driving time it will take LightQueen to drive along it in either direction.
103558	Some intersections connect to many roads, but the average number of roads at any intersection
103559	is less than 5. LightQueen needs to get from Carburetor Falls at intersection s to the SparkPlug
103560	Derby race track at intersection t, subject to the following conditions:
103561	• LightQueen’s gas tank has a positive integer capacity g < n: it can hold up to g units of gas
103562	at a time (starting full). Along the way, she can refill her tank (by any integer amount) at any
103563	intersection marked with a gas station. It takes exactly tG time for her to fill up 1 unit of gas.
103564	5 Problem Set 6
103565	• LightQueen uses gas only when driving uphill. Specifically, if she drives on a road from
103566	intersection xi to xj at elevations ei and ej respectively, LightQueen will use exactly ej − ei
103567	units of gas to travel along it if ej > ei, and will use zero units of gas otherwise.
103568	Given LightQueen’s map, describe an O(n2 log n)-time algorithm to return a fastest route to the
103569	race that keeps a strictly positive amount of gas in her tank at all times (if such a route exists).
103570	Solution: Create a graph G:
103571	• Vertices: for each intersection v, add a vertex vi for every i ∈ {1, . . . , g}, where vertex vi
103572	represents being at intersection v with i units of gasoline in her tank; and
103573	• Edges: for each bi-directional road {u, v} connecting intersections u and v with driving time
103574	t(u, v) (let e(u) and e(v) be the elevations of intersections u and v respectively, and without
103575	loss of generality assume e(u) ≤ e(v)), construct the following directed edges:
103576	1. (Down-hill Road Edges)
103577	– add a weight-t(u, v) edge (vi, ui) for every i ∈ {1, . . . g} (since traveling in this
103578	direction on the road requires no gas).
103579	2. (Up-hill Road Edges)
103580	– if e(u) == e(v), add another weight-t(u, v) edge opposite the previous, specifically:
103581	(ui, vi) for every i ∈ {1, . . . , g};
103582	– otherwise e(v) − e(u) = ` > 0, so add a weight-t(u, v) edge (ui, vi−`) for every
103583	i ∈ {` + 1, . . . , g} (since traveling uphill costs gas, and she is not allowed to ever
103584	run out of gas).
103585	3. (Gas Station Edges)
103586	– for each gas station, e.g., at intersection v, add a weight-tG edge (vi, vi+1) for every
103587	i ∈ {1, . . . , g − 1} (corresponding to filling up the tank by one unit at the station).
103588	There are gr Down-hill Road Edges, at most gr Up-hill Road Edges, and at most (g − 1)n Gas
103589	Station Edges, so graph G has gn vertices and O(g(r +n)) edges. This graph has the property that
103590	any path from vertex sg to any vertex ti for i ∈ {1, . . . , g} will be a valid route for LightQueen
103591	to leave Carburetor Falls with a full tank and reach SparkPlug Derby without ever running out of
103592	gas along the way; and the path’s weight corresponds to the time it would take her to get there. So
103593	solve SSSP from sg to find a minimum weight path to each ti for i ∈ {1, . . . , g}, and return a path
103594	to one with minimum weight (or return no such path exists). This graph may contain cycles, but
103595	has only positive edge weights, so solve SSSP using Dijkstra.
103596	Since the average degree of each intersection is < 5 and every road connects two intersections, then
103597	2r < 5n and r = O(n). Since g < n by the problem statement, G has O(n2) vertices and O(n2)
103598	edges, so takes O(n2) time to construct. Then Dijkstra takes O(n2 log(n2) + n2) = O(n2 log n)
103599	time, while finding the minimum path to any ti takes O(n) time, leading to O(n2 log n) time in
103600	total, as desired.
103601	Rubric:
103602	6 Problem Set 6
103603	• 6 points for construction of a graph that can be used to solve the problem
103604	• 3 points for description of a correct algorithm
103605	• 2 points for a correct argument of correctness
103606	• 3 points for a correct argument of running time
103607	• 6 points if correct algorithm is efficient, i.e., O(n2 log n)-time
103608	• Partial credit may be awarded

103623	Problem 6-6. [25 points] Johnson’s Algorithm
103624	In this problem, you will implement Johnson’s Algorithm to compute all-pairs shortest-path weights
103625	in a general weighted directed graph G, as described in Lecture 14. The input to your algorithm
103626	will be: a positive integer n representing the number of vertices of your graph identified by con￾secutive integers 0 to n − 1, and a tuple S of triples, where each triple (u, v,w) corresponds to a
103627	directed edge from vertex u to v of weight w. Your output should be a length-n tuple D of length-n
103628	tuples where D[u][v] = δ(u, v) for all u, v ∈ {0, . . . , n − 1}, except when the input graph contains
103629	a negative-weight cycle when you should return None.
103630	Please implement the johnson(n, S) function in the template code provided. Your code tem￾plate contains working implementations of Bellman–Ford and Dijkstra (using a binary heap as a
103631	priority queue) modified from the recitation notes. Note that you will have to construct your own
103632	adjacency list and weight function if you would like to use this code. You can download the code
103633	template and some test cases from the website.
103634	Solution:
103635	1 INF = 99999 # distance magnitudes will not be larger than this number
103636	2
103637	3 def johnson(n, S):
103638	4 D = [[INF for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(n)]
103639	5 Adj = [[] for _ in range(n)] # construct graph
103640	6 W = {}
103641	7 for (u, v, w) in S:
103642	8 Adj[u].append(v)
103643	9 W[(u, v)] = w
103644	10 Adj.append([i for i in range(n)]) # run bellman-ford from supernode
103645	11 for i in range(n):
103646	12 W[(n, i)] = 0
103647	13 def wf(u, v): return W[(u, v)]
103648	14 args = bellman_ford(Adj, wf, n)
103649	15 if args is None:
103650	16 return None
103651	17 h, _ = args
103652	18 def wf(u, v): return W[(u, v)] + h[u] - h[v]
103653	19 for u in range(n): # compute SSSP
103654	20 d, parent = dijkstra(Adj, wf, u)
103655	21 for v in range(n):
103656	22 if d[v] < INF:
103657	23 D[u][v] = d[v] - h[u] + h[v]
103658	24 return tuple(tuple(row) for row in D)
103659	on reweighted graph
